title: In a World Gone Wild, Why Care About Student Motivation
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart makes the case for why student motivation deserves serious professional attention rather than being dismissed as dry PD content or reduced to blaming unmotivated kids. He gives three reasons: demotivation is genuinely painful, not just for students but for the teachers and parents around them; school is structurally impossible without motivation, since mastery of complex disciplines requires sustained, careful effort that only happens when students care; and motivation is unusually malleable compared to other fundamental drivers of student outcomes, since research shows it responds directly to the signals, actions, and experiences teachers provide in the classroom. He acknowledges other equally fundamental factors, such as knowledge-rich curricula, stable home environments, and equitable access, but argues teachers have outsized influence specifically over motivation because it operates within their daily reach. The piece serves as a rationale-setting companion to his forthcoming book on the topic, explaining why he has hunkered down on motivation as his central professional focus.
points: Reframes demotivation as a soul experiencing pain rather than a discipline problem, arguing this shift in framing changes how teachers should respond to disengaged students.
Argues motivation isn't a soft add-on to instruction but a structural precondition for school itself, since mastery requires sustained work done with care.

Distinguishes motivation from other fundamental outcome drivers, like curriculum quality, home environment, and equity of access, by noting research shows it's uniquely responsive to teacher-controlled signals and actions.
Explicitly rejects the carrots-and-sticks and blame-the-student framings of motivation that he says have made many teachers dismiss it as a serious area of study.
quotes: We have bad associations with the term "student motivation," likening it to attitudes that blame low performance on students (they just didn't care enough, they weren't motivated enough, they were lazy) or schemes that basically boil down to carrots and sticks.

We pay too little attention to the fact that we've never a day in our lives woken up and said, "Today I'd like to not care about things, to be jaded, to be disengaged, to be against what I'll be required to do." Humans like being motivated.

And, conversely, we're in pain when what we're doing seems pointless, irrelevant, or hopeless. So the next time you see a student who is demotivated, you have to remind yourself, "Okay. This is a soul experiencing pain.

The trouble with that purpose, though, is the word "master" — human beings can't grow in mastery of things as complex as our arts and disciplines without doing certain work and doing that work with care (attention, curiosity, zeal, resilience).

What makes student motivation special among all these, however, is that the research clearly demonstrates that, at least when they are with us in our classrooms, student motivation is greatly influenced by the signals we do or don't send, the actions we do or don't take, the experiences we do or don't facilitate.
But for real, we are a big deal when it comes to this topic. We affect it a lot more than we think we do.
